analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid and CHIP to cover COVID-19 vaccines and treatment with no out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in committee with zero cosponsors until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) to require coverage of COVID-19 vaccines and treatment, including care for conditions that complicate COVID-19, with no copays or other cost-sharing for families. It also would have added COVID-19 vaccines to the Vaccines for Children program, which provides free shots to uninsured and underinsured children 18 and under. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income children and families covered by Medicaid or CHIP, who would get COVID-19 vaccines, treatment, and related care without paying anything out of pocket, and uninsured children who get shots through the Vaccines for Children program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income kids on Medicaid and CHIP

how_it_helps.text: Adds COVID-19 vaccines and their administration, plus COVID-19 treatment services, to the list of items Medicaid must cover, and bars Medicaid cost-sharing for them, including in territories.

Requires CHIP to cover COVID-19 vaccines and treatment, including treatment for conditions that may complicate COVID-19, for targeted low-income children, and prohibits CHIP cost-sharing for those services.
Adds COVID-19 vaccines to the Vaccines for Children program, entitling vaccine-eligible children to receive them from registered providers at no charge for the vaccine or its administration.
The changes would have taken effect on enactment and applied to a COVID-19 vaccine beginning on the date it is licensed, so coverage would not wait for the end of the pandemic emergency.

analysis.who_pays: State Medicaid and CHIP programs (with their usual federal matching funds) and the federal Vaccines for Children program would bear the added cost of buying and covering vaccines and treatment; Medicaid managed-care plans would have to include the no-cost-sharing services in their coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicaid, CHIP, and the federal vaccine program

drawbacks.text: The mandate is an added cost for state Medicaid and CHIP budgets and for the federal government, which would pay for free childhood COVID-19 vaccines through the Vaccines for Children program.

The CHIP cost-sharing piece overlapped with protections Congress had already passed: the bill text amends section 2103(e)(2) 'as amended by section 6004(b)(3) of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act,' which had already prohibited CHIP cost-sharing for testing-related visits, so part of the bill extended rather than created that protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: it would have guaranteed that children and families on Medicaid and CHIP could get COVID-19 shots and treatment without a bill attached, which matters because even small copays lead low-income families to skip care. The cost is real but modest and spread across state and federal budgets, and it is the same kind of no-cost-sharing protection that private insurance was already required to provide for COVID-19 vaccines during the pandemic. The design is narrow and straightforward; the main honest criticism is that it duplicated protections that other legislation was already putting in place for some groups.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Chris Pappas of New Hampshire introduced the bill on February 2, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On February 3, 2021, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Health, which is where its action history ends.
The bill drew no cosponsors during the two years of the 117th Congress.
No further action was taken and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No constituency won anything. Low-income families gained no new coverage guarantee, while state Medicaid budgets and insurers were spared the added mandate; the committee simply never acted.

for.name: Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it to the House, where it was referred to committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Frank Pallone)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire 117th Congress without a markup, hearing, or vote; its Health Subcommittee took no action after the February 3, 2021 referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split exists in the record; the Democratic sponsor drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Managed-care plans that cover most Medicaid enrollees would have to include COVID-19 vaccines and treatment without cost-sharing in their coverage, a modest added obligation. Families would see no bills for COVID-19 care.

Medicaid, CHIP, and the federal Vaccines for Children program would have purchased COVID-19 vaccines and paid for their administration, creating a guaranteed public payer for the product. The public benefit (free shots for kids) and the industry benefit (reimbursed sales) run together.
